items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer — people resist change for several different reasons:**

**(a)** People generally ask **"What's in it for me?"** — meaning, by going through these changes, **what will I gain out of it**.
**(b)** Many people are **afraid to adapt or learn new things, especially technology, when they are not IT savvy**.
**(c)** A few, although ready to learn a new skill, resist because **they think this new skill may not be useful later**.
**(d)** Some are **afraid of their status after the ERP project ends** — whether their job will be retained, or their role.
**(e)** Some are **anxious about using the new system**, and hence resist.

**The deck adds two more:** *"What will be my new role? Will it be different work / more work?"* and *"Do I need to go back to my old place after the project? What will I do there?"*

**Group them as three fears for recall — Job, System, Payoff:**

| Fear | Questions |
|---|---|
| **Fear for the job** | new role · will my job remain · back to my old place |
| **Fear of the system** | can I operate it · can I cope with new technology |
| **Doubt about the payoff** | what's in it for me · will my new skill be valued |

**Worth adding for full marks:** the resistance is **rational, not irrational**. The twelve ERP benefits accrue to the *organization*; the individual gets more work. Reason (c) is a genuine **investment calculation** about the transferability of the skill — which is why the remedies are **incentives and new roles**, not persuasion.

items.q: **What are the different strategies to handle change?**
items.answer:
**The strategy has two levels.**

**Level 1 — Handle fear and uncertainty** *(the QnA: "for this, **communication is the key**")*
- **Communicate**
- **Training** — addresses *unknown aspects, fear of ignorance* and *"how it can help me"*
- **A team of Power users and ERP champions** — *able to demonstrate benefits and resolve issues in a congenial way*
- **Round the clock (24×7) help desk** — *people want help for trivial things to complicated issues, almost any time of the day*
- **Leadership support**

**Level 2 — Getting motivated and committed** *(the QnA: "for this, **organizational design is the key**")*
- **Involve employees in each critical ERP decision and discussion**
- **Design incentive schemes and performance measures** — *people need incentives to adopt new ways of working*
- **Design new and more interesting roles**

**The order matters and is worth stating:** Level 1 **removes the negatives**, Level 2 **adds the positives**. You cannot skip to Level 2 — **a frightened employee cannot be motivated**.

**The deck's sharp observation on the Level-1 measures:** they *"directly help, plus indirectly remove some of the **'insincere' efforts to avoid change**"* — the excuses *"I was never trained"*, *"nobody helped me"*, *"no seniors see it"*. Each measure closes one excuse.

**On Level 2**, the deck divides people into three groups — the **self-motivated**, those **motivated for not so desirable reasons**, and the largest group who want to see clearly **"what's in it for me."** The three strategies target the third group. As the deck puts it: ***"One can take the horse to the water…"***

items.q: **What is Organizational Design in the context of ERP? Describe the Change Team.**
items.answer:
**ORGANIZATIONAL DESIGN**

New technology has an impact on the structure of the organization, through a cascade:

$$\textbf{New technology} \rightarrow \textbf{new processes} \rightarrow \textbf{new roles} \rightarrow \textbf{new structure} \rightarrow \textbf{new measures \& incentives}$$

**Organizational design means:** new/defined **roles and responsibilities** · new/defined **reporting structure** · **job descriptions** · new/defined **performance measures and incentive systems**, which *"can play an enormous role in determining and reinforcing desired behaviours."*

**The stated objective — learn verbatim:**
> *"**The architecture of the organization needs to be aligned with the new process and technology.**"*

**THE CHANGE TEAM**

| | **Core Change Team** | **Extended Change Team** |
|---|---|---|
| **Does** | implements organizational change management steps | introduces and conducts **risk assessments**, communicates, implements action plans |
| **Reports to** | **Project Sponsor and Manager** | — |
| **Who** | **dedicated** — HR, OD professionals and/or consulting | **part-time** — line management or consulting |
| **Composition** | ideally a **mix of long and short-term employees** | — |

**Change Team Lead** — *"must know the organization well and be **well-respected** within it… will become the **symbolic face** of the organizational change management program. Therefore the more **credibility** he/she holds, the better."*

**Two points worth adding:** the change teams are **generally not part of the primary implementation team** — they are *"organization change agents"*. And the ASAP role chart's six **"points"** (Knowledge Transfer, Risk Assessment, Skills Development, Communications, Sponsorship, Organizational Optimization) are **shared duties, not six dedicated people** — one per ASAP change process.

**Remember them as A SOCKS:**

| Process | Definition | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Assessment** | **Uncovering and prioritizing risks** | *identify and prioritize handling of **perception*** |
| **S — Sponsorship** | **Gaining & demonstrating leadership support** | messages and support from top management are **visible & timely** — ***not just lip-service*** |
| **O — Organizational optimization** | **Aligning jobs and processes with the new business environment** | promote and propose organizational changes in line with new ERP processes; **create roles and incentive structure**; resolve issues |
| **C — Communications** | **Designing and delivering key messages** | **regular · different mediums · customized to stakeholders · framework of communication** |
| **K — Knowledge transfer** | **Capturing and sharing lessons learned** | methods and means of KT across the organization; **track requisite knowledge of the project** |
| **S — Skills development** | **Org change management training** | **big-picture**, understanding and communicating new processes, dealing with different stakeholders |

**Two structural points for full marks:**

**Communications spans the other five** — *"communication spans across the other 5, but has its own focus as well."* Every other process produces something that must be communicated, yet the strategy and framework are work in their own right.

**Skills Development is *not* end-user ERP training.** It teaches the **change agents** — big picture, communicating new processes, handling stakeholders. End-user training on the software is a separate activity in Final Preparation.

**The deck's stated ambition for the whole set:** ***"Make people welcome the change and ask for it."*** Compliance is not the target — **Assessment, Sponsorship and Communications** work on Level-1 fear, while **Skills Development, Knowledge Transfer and Organizational Optimization** work on Level-2 commitment.

items.q: **What is a business process? Give examples. What are the fundamental principles of business processes?**
items.answer:
**Definition (QnA):**
> *"A business process is a **set of logically related tasks** that use the **resources of an organization** to achieve a **defined business outcome** or goal or objective."*

**(a)** A process has a **clear beginning and an end**, and **clearly identified inputs and outputs**.
**(b)** Processes are **cross-functional and not restricted within a single function**.

**The four principles:**
1. **A process has a number of steps**
2. **Each step has specific input and output**
3. **Each step can be run by a separate organizational entity / department / person**
4. **Each step should add value to the whole process**

**Examples** — the typical high-level processes named for BPR selection: **Order Fulfillment Process (OFP)** · **Procure to Pay (PTP)** · **Demand generation** · **Product Development Process (PDP)** · **Employee Hire to Retire**.

**Worked example of a process spanning departments — Order Management:** Sales *(order entry, pricing)* → Production *(manufacture, hand to Quality)* → Quality *(inspect to customer spec, move to finished goods)* → Warehouse *(pick from stock)* → Distribution/Transport *(deliver)* → Finance *(invoicing, payment)*.

**Two points worth adding:**

**Principle 4 is the one that makes BPR possible** — it is a *test*: a step that adds no value is a candidate for elimination, which generates the whole **Value Added / Non-Value Added / Waste** classification.

**Because a process spans departments, its efficiency depends on all contributing departments** — which is why no single department can reengineer it, and why the BPR team needs a **Steering Committee** to *settle inter-process disputes*.

items.q: **What is BPR? What are the three important concepts of BPR? Why is BPR needed?**
items.answer:
**DEFINITION (Michael Hammer) — learn verbatim:**
> *"A **fundamental rethinking** and **radical redesign** of business processes to achieve **dramatic improvements** in critical, contemporary measures of performance — such as **cost, quality, service, and speed**."*

**THE THREE IMPORTANT CONCEPTS:**

| Concept | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Fundamental rethinking** | **BPR is not about doing small changes; it is all about a new way of thinking to do the process** |
| **Radical redesign** | **The new process should look very different from the old one** |
| **Dramatic improvements** | **A reengineered process can bring significant improvement in process performance in terms of cost, time or service performance** |

**Mnemonic — BPR is FRD**, and the three are a chain rather than synonyms:
$$\underbrace{\textbf{Fundamental}}_{\text{how you } think} \rightarrow \underbrace{\textbf{Radical}}_{\text{what you } design} \rightarrow \underbrace{\textbf{Dramatic}}_{\text{what you } achieve}$$

**WHY BPR IS NEEDED (QnA):**
**(a)** the **outer world is changing constantly** — business is changing, technology is improving in leaps and bounds
**(b)** **stakeholder expectations are rising** day by day
**(c)** **competition is very high**
**(d)** need to **innovate, bring out break-through products**
**(e)** **execute processes faster and cheaper**

The deck's five forces are: **external world changing (business) · external world changing (technology) · components of business execution changing (people, machines, infrastructure) · business stakeholder expectations · competition changes and challenges** — *"only thing that is constant in this world is change!"*

**Worth adding:** four of the five forces are **outside the organisation's control**, so a process decays as the environment moves even when nobody does anything wrong. Hence the deck's conclusion — ***"any organization which has been running stable for a while without much organizational changes is a potential candidate for BPR."***

**Also note the caveat:** the deck states Hammer's definition is **dated** — *"since modern businesses are already on good business practices, the terms **radical & dramatic may have to be toned down**."*

items.q: **What are the pros and cons of BPR? What are the keys to its success?**
items.answer:
**PROS (8):** Enterprise Integration · Empowered Employee · **No Handoff** · Simplified Process · Less Coordination and Reconciliation · **Reduce NVA, Eliminate Waste** · **Case Manager as SPOC** · Effective Use of IT

**CONS (5):** **High Failure Rate** · Can take a long time · Can consume a lot of organizational resources (costs, executive time) · **Can make existing jobs redundant** · **High Resistance to change**

**KEYS TO SUCCESS (6):**
1. **Leadership and top management commitment in the project**
2. **Prototype every process before large scale implementation**
3. **Show early success within the first three to six months**
4. **Results to be measurable**
5. **Communicate effectively to manage change**
6. **Proper change management**

**Deck's note: *"Leadership must believe in the new system."***

**Three analytical points that lift the answer:**

**Most pros follow from one move — removing hand-offs.** *No handoff → simplified process → less coordination and reconciliation → reduced NVA.* Every handoff needs a queue, a check and a reconciliation, so removing it removes all three. **Case Manager as SPOC** is the mechanism, **empowered employee** and **IT** are the enablers.

**Cons 4 and 5 are cause and effect.** BPR *"can make existing jobs redundant"* — that is what *radical redesign* and *eliminate waste* mean when the waste is a person's job. Therefore *"high resistance to change"* is entirely rational, and *proper change management* is a key to success rather than a nicety.

**Four of the six keys map directly onto a named reason for failure** — top management commitment ↔ *no top management support*; prototyping ↔ *large scale implementation without prototyping*; measurable results ↔ Gartner's *70% of failed projects did not use performance metrics*; communication and change management ↔ *ignore people concerns*.

items.q: **Why does BPR fail? Explain the reasons.**
items.answer:
**The eight stated reasons:**
1. **Too much AS IS Analysis (Paralysis)**
2. **Poor Scoping**
3. **Ignore People Concerns**
4. **Not putting best people in the project**
5. **Little change in process — Not redesign**
6. **Looking for a sure success recipe** *(copy design from another successful BPR project, blindly)*
7. **Large scale implementation without prototyping**
8. **No Top Management Support**

**Group them as Analysis, People, Execution (A-P-E):** analysis errors (1, 2) · people errors (3, 4, 8) · design and execution errors (5, 6, 7). **The people family is the largest**, consistent with *organizational change is difficult because of "human" elements, mostly.*

**The three worth explaining in detail:**

**1 — Too much AS-IS analysis.** The As-Is model is *required*, so the failure is over-doing it. The correct depth is stated in the BPM chapter: *"no need of much detailed analysis as anyway the process will not be used in future"* — high level only. **AS-IS shallow, TO-BE deep.** Teams get it backwards because the As-Is is observable and documenting it *feels* like progress.

**5 — Little change, not redesign.** This is BPR failing by not being BPR: a project that tinkers has done **TQM** while paying BPR's costs. The deck's proverb: ***"Old process + new technology = costly old process."***

**6 — Copying another design blindly.** A redesign that worked elsewhere was fitted to *that* company's products, customers and constraints, and arrives without the reasoning that produced it. Worse, **a copied process cannot differentiate you** — someone else already has it. This is why *organization mission, vision, values & culture* is a **key input to redesign**: the principles are universal, but **the design is local**.

items.q: **What are the phases of a BPR project? Describe the reengineering team and its roles.**
items.answer:
**THE PHASES** — *"Select The Doctor, Redesign, Prototype, Implement"*:
1. **Selection of the process to be redesigned**
2. **Have the reengineering team in place**
3. **Process Diagnosis**
4. **Process Redesign**
5. **Prototyping**
6. **Full Scale Implementation**

*Diagnosis before redesign is non-negotiable — prescribing before diagnosing is failure reason 5. Prototyping is a distinct phase, not an optional extra.*

**THE SIX ROLES — 2 leaders, 2 doers, 2 coordinators:**

**1. Leader** *(= the Project Manager)* — **identifies the key business processes** · **appoints senior managers as Process owners** · **creates environment by motivating & supporting** · **establishes measures of performance and rewards** · **articulates and communicates the need to reengineer**

**2. Steering Committee** — **settle issues outside the scope of individual processes** · **determine order of priority** · **allocation of resources** · **settlement of inter-process disputes**

**3. Process Owner** *(technical subject matter expert)* — **appoints the reengineering team** · **obtains resources** · **motivates, inspires and advises** · **supports and protects radically new ideas** · **manages the process once reengineering is over**

**4. Reengineering Team** — **produce ideas and plans and debate them exhaustively** · **redesign the process** · **sell the designed process to the people** · **continue through to implementation**

**5. Reengineering Coordinator** — advise the leader on the **"hard" part** · coordinate ongoing activities · **provide common approaches** · help select insiders and outsiders · **monitor the Process owner** · anticipate and develop infrastructure

**6. Change Coordinator** — helps fashion the **change management programme** · follows up on implementation · **tests and reports periodically the reactions of the rest of the folks** · ***"conscience keeper of the leader"***

**Points worth adding:** three of the Steering Committee's four duties are about **resolving conflict**, because processes cross departments and no process owner can settle a dispute with another department. The **Process Owner is permanent** — *"manages the process once reengineering is over"* — which fixes the diagnosed problem of *"clear ownership of process missing."* And roles **could be merged and played by fewer individuals**; six roles means six *responsibilities*, not six people.

items.q: **Explain the process selection and process diagnosis phases of BPR.**
items.answer:
**PROCESS SELECTION**

Start from a **list of high level processes** — *"not all activities are processes."* Typical ones: **Order Fulfillment (OFP) · Procure to Pay (PTP) · Demand generation · Product Development (PDP) · Hire to Retire.**

**Three decision factors:**
1. **Based on benchmarking** — an **external** yardstick: *where are we worse than others?*
2. **Unsatisfactory / troubled processes** — an **internal** yardstick: *where does it hurt?*
3. **Potential for quick results** — a **political** yardstick, operationalising the key to success *"show early success within three to six months."*

**PROCESS DIAGNOSIS AND ANALYSIS**

**Steps:** understand steps in the current process (inputs, outputs) → **categorize the steps into Value Added, Non Value Added and Waste** → **record the time for each step** and how the information system is used → understand issues → **for each issue, examine the rules and assumptions behind it**

**Key analysis criteria:** understand **rules and assumptions** · assess input/output value to the end result **as seen by the customer** · identify key steps and parameters · list specific issues

**The seven NVA activities** — four kinds of waste: **Storing** and **Moving** *(logistics)* · **Checks & controls** and **Inspection** *(control)* · **Reworking** and **Reconciliation** *(failure)* · **Expediting** *(urgency)*.

**Common process problems:** no **end-to-end ownership** · **too many hand-offs** · **wrong measurements — task performance rather than process performance** · **sequential execution of steps** · large numbers of audits and reconciliations adding no customer value · very few steps value-adding.

**Why processes end up this way:** non-availability of technology in the beginning · **process copied from another company/parent org** · **brought in as a temporary measure but never reviewed** · **process there to suit some set of individuals**.

**Two points that lift the answer:**

**"Record the time for each step"** is what makes *dramatic improvement* provable rather than asserted — you cannot claim a speed improvement without a baseline.

**NVA is not the same as useless.** The deck cautions: *"even though most of these do not add value, they **may have some value such as management information**. One needs to separate this and **retain / transfer this in some other step**."*

items.q: **Explain the principles of process redesign, the Case Manager concept and the levers of redesign.**
items.answer:
**THE TEN PRINCIPLES:** **SPOC for process · combine several jobs into one · multiple versions · simplify process · reduce audits · workers make decisions · coaches · maximize VA · parallelize work · process teams**

*Deck's caution: "principles are fairly broad. **Redesign needs good thinking, innovation, vision and practicality.**"*

**Each principle answers a diagnosed problem:** too many hand-offs → **SPOC, combine jobs, process teams**; sequential execution → **parallelize**; too many audits → **reduce audits, workers make decisions**; few value-adding steps → **maximize VA, simplify**; no ownership → **SPOC, coaches**; one rigid process → **multiple versions**.

**THE CASE MANAGER — a Single Point Of Contact (SPOC) for a process:**

| | Flow |
|---|---|
| **Before** | Credit request → Financing → Credit checking → Approval → Issuance → Credit decision |
| **After** | Credit request → **Case manager** → Credit decision |

**Four departments become one role.** Three hand-offs vanish, and with each a queue, a status enquiry and a reconciliation. *"SPOC acts as a good interface between parties and should be **highly approachable and responsive**."* **It is only possible because IT gives one person the information four departments used to hold** — the human-facing consequence of enterprise integration.

**HAMMER'S PROCESS-CENTERED ORGANIZATION:** *"there is a **process owner** for each process, and process owners depend on several **centers of excellence** for bringing competency into the process. Each such COE can be managed by a **coach**."* Processes run **horizontally toward customers**; centres of excellence run **vertically** holding specialist skill — a matrix in which the functional dimension survives as a *skills home* but is no longer the axis of delivery.

**THE LEVERS OF PROCESS REDESIGN:** **roles and responsibilities** · **measurements and incentives — at process level rather than individual functional** · **Information Technology** · **organizational structure — flattened hierarchy** · **skills — multi-skilling**

*They are **interdependent**, so you switch over in stages: "set the levers in 1-2-2 state, stabilize the system; shift to higher levels 3-4-4… stabilize there."*

**Key inputs to redesign:** **stated principles · external consultants · organization mission, vision, values & culture · possibility of a prototype and its results.** On consultants: *"**insiders are always 'biased' by virtue of being in the system for long**, so external involvement is always beneficial."*

items.q: **Compare BPR with TQM. Why is prototyping necessary before full implementation?**
items.answer:
**BPR vs TQM:**

| Parameter | **Process Improvement / TQM** | **Process Redesign / BPR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Level of change** | **Incremental** | **Radical** |
| **Starting point** | **Existing process** | **Clean slate** |
| **Frequency of change** | **Continuous** | **One-time** |
| **Time required** | Short term | Long term |
| **Participation** | **Bottom up** | **Top down** |
| **Typical scope** | Narrow | Broad |
| **Risk** | Moderate | **High** |
| **Primary enabler** | **Statistical control** | **IT** |
| **Type of change** | Cultural | **Cultural / Structural** |

**The graph is the memory hook:** plotting process performance against time, **TQM is a gentle upward slope** — small gains continuously — while **BPR is a step change** — a jump, then a plateau. *"Performance improvement in BPR is quite drastic; in TQM it is a slow graph."*

**Every row follows from that shape.** A *step* must be radical, from a clean slate, and happens once — hence long to prepare and high risk, since you get one attempt. A *slope* is incremental, starts from the existing process, and is continuous — hence short, narrow, moderate risk. **Participation follows too:** a step change must be **top down** because only management can authorise structural change; a slope is **bottom up** because the people doing the work spot the small improvements.

**They are not alternatives** — *"a company might be running more than one improvement programme at any time… but they overlap with BPR."* The natural relationship is sequential: BPR delivers the step, TQM works the slope upward from the new level.

**PROTOTYPING** — *"initially run the new process on a small 'set' — few customers, few transactions."* It **helps decide the organization support/structure needed** and **helps in detailing the process correctly**.

**Why it is necessary:** *"though a lot of thinking goes into creating a new process, **some unexpected issues might crop up while implementing**. So a prototype phase is a must to check **viability** and to some extent **acceptance of the people involved**. **Only after the prototype is run successfully can all the points be frozen.**"*

It settles **three questions at once** — does it work, will people accept it, and what does it need. The second is what distinguishes a BPR prototype from a software pilot.

items.q: **What is Business Engineering? Explain benchmarking and best practices, and the relationship between BPR and ERP.**
items.answer:
**BUSINESS ENGINEERING**
$$\textbf{BE} = \textbf{BPR} + \textbf{IT}$$

**IT changes the rules of business — disruptive:** **data available anywhere to anybody with control** · **software enables even a non-expert to do an expert job** · **decision support tools for everybody** · **plans get revised instantaneously**

*Caveat worth stating: **"BPR is possible without IT also!"** — the equation is a scoping statement for the ERP context, not a definition of BPR.*

**BENCHMARKING** — *"the process of **comparing one's business processes and performance metrics to industry bests** and/or best practices from other industries."*

**Five types:** **Process** *(business processes, observing best practices from benchmark companies)* · **Financial** *(financial analysis to assess competitiveness and productivity in money terms)* · **Competitiveness** *(comparing products and services with target firms)* · **Product** *(designing new products or upgrades)* · **Functional** *(a single function, e.g. HR)*

**Steps:** identify focus area → identify **leaders / competition / standards** → identify measures / best practices → **align & implement suitable practices**

**Exemplars:** **Toyota — Just-in-Time (JIT)** · **Motorola — Six Sigma** · **Wal-Mart — Vendor Managed Inventory (VMI)**

**Pitfalls:** *"any benchmarking has many known **'games' and pitfalls — comparing 'apples' to 'oranges'**."* Where no external yardstick exists, companies **compare to themselves at a different period** — honest about like-for-like, but it can never tell you whether you are competitive.

**BEST PRACTICES** — one of the reasons to bring in ERP. They arrive **in the form of: specific processes · pre-configured settings · business blueprints · test process & data · master data.** They come **from leading corporations** *(Kanban/JIT — Toyota; VMI — Wal-Mart)*, **industry group initiatives**, and **ERP vendors' experience**. SAP's offer is **industry specific, cross industry, and a baseline package**.

*Caution: "**many times vendors force fit some of the not-so-great features also as best practices**" — and "it is a little tricky to pinpoint best practice."*

**BPR AND ERP — the middle path.** Risks of full-blown BPR before ERP: it takes long time and cost; **there is no guarantee the best-designed processes will be supported by the ERP solution**; it may take 3–4 years, by which time business dynamics change.

**Most favour the middle path** — follow the **best practice processes that come with the ERP**, and do a **limited BPR** where it gives **competitive advantage**.

**The counter-risk:** *"strong bias towards ERP driven best practice… **may lead to losing competitive advantage**. So BPR team/implementers need to look for **differentiators**. Do not lose out on the company's special competence."*

**The rule in one line: standardise where you don't compete; differentiate where you do.**

items.q: **Why is business process modelling important in an ERP project? Give some rules of process modelling.**
items.answer:
**IMPORTANCE (QnA's model answer):**

*Since it is a **visual model** it becomes **easy to understand for people who are new to the project** and need to understand the procedure followed in this company. It quickly shows the **activities of a process, the steps involved and all the activities under it**. This helps in **identifying improvement areas** in the current process. It will help to **quickly navigate from Scenario to Process to Activity to Step**. Hence it is a very useful **communication mechanism across different stakeholders**, and it helps to **bridge the gap between the business team and the IT team**.*

**The deck's fuller list adds:** a **quick comparison of AS IS and TO BE** when both are represented · **very useful to check the impact of changes** at any particular step/activity · **tool driven** · and it identifies **points of hand-offs and unnecessary steps that can be eliminated or parallelized**.

**Lead with the IT–business bridge** — *"bridges the gap between IT people and business users who generally do not speak the same language."* The business expert knows the process but not the system; the consultant knows the system but not the business. **A diagram is a shared artefact both can read.**

**THE RULES (QnA — "any number below based on the marks"):**
1. **Each process should have specific inputs and outputs**
2. **Each process should cross a number of functional boundaries**
3. **Differentiate between the means** (forms, documents, procedures) **and the end** (value added, deliverables). *There can always be a different way of doing the process if the process goals are met.* **Focus on goals more than means**
4. **Processes should relate to customers and their needs**, directly or as contributors to other processes
5. **Process Map creation must be evolved by a cross functional team**
6. **Assume no organizational structure or boundaries**
7. **Think outside all constraints**

**Rules 6 and 7 are the operational heart.** If you draw the To-Be process **as departments currently exist**, you reproduce the current hand-offs — because the boundaries *generate* the hand-offs. **The org chart must not be an input to the process design.**

*Note the limitation: **"BPM will have to be supported with textual documentation wherever required"*** — and keeping diagram and notes **in sync is a known problem.**

items.q: **What is AS-IS and TO-BE modelling? Define their purpose. Explain the business process hierarchy.**
items.answer:
**AS-IS MODELLING**
**Purpose:** *"understand current processes for the purpose of **improving**"* — the QnA adds: the process followed **before ERP implementation**.
**Guiding principles:** **no need of much detailed analysis, as anyway the process will not be used in future** · it is important to understand the process **at high level** — **why the process exists · what it does · what's the high level objective**

**TO-BE MODELLING**
**Purpose:** **new process design** — the procedures to be followed **using the ERP implementation**.
**Guiding principles:** **needs to be detailed so that every step is clear to users** · **all input–output relationships, data flows, and the organization roles performing the process need to be detailed out**

**The asymmetry is the point: AS-IS shallow, TO-BE deep.** Getting it backwards is BPR failure reason 1, *analysis paralysis*.

**But shallow is not careless** — *"**if you do not understand where you are, any detailed map is pretty much useless!** … often As-Is is based on a critical set of understanding/assumptions. It is important to **understand and document them as well**."*

**Why TO-BE must be detailed:** it is what gets **configured into the ERP** during Realization. A vague To-Be produces guesses at configuration time. And **comparing the two models is gap analysis.**

**THE BUSINESS PROCESS HIERARCHY** — *"a logical grouping of **Business Scenarios, Business Processes, Activities and Steps**"* — mnemonic **SPAS**:

| Level | Name | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Scenario** | Supply Chain Management |
| **2** | **Process** | Order Management |
| **3** | **Activity** | Delivery Scheduling |
| **4** | **Step** | Calculation of Delivery Date |

**Why a hierarchy?** *"Business processes can be many"* — 40 to 100 even in a medium-sized company. It **helps see processes at different levels** · lets people **explode and analyze based on their organizational role** · makes it **easy to navigate from Scenario to Process to Activity to Step** · and makes it **easy to define roles at different levels**.

*The deck's notes add: hierarchy **facilitates control and intuitive structure when the numbers are larger**, gives **natural delegation of responsibility and consolidation of goals**, and **facilitates abstraction**.*

**One model, read at four depths by four audiences** — and it is what makes *"process owner"* a definable job, since ownership is assigned **at a level**.

items.q: **Describe the business process definition standards, and the dimensions of a process model.**
items.answer:
**THE FOUR FAMILIES**, ordered by scope:

| Family | Standard |
|---|---|
| **Enterprise Process Standard** | **APQC Process Classification Framework** *(American Productivity and Quality Council)* |
| **Supply Chain Process Standard** | **SCOR — Supply Chain Operation Reference Model** |
| **Industry Process Standards** | **ECR** *(Efficient Consumer Response)* in retail |
| **Collaboration Process Standards** | **VICS** *(Voluntary Intra-Industry Commerce Standards)* |

**APQC** splits an enterprise into **Operation Processes (1–7)** — manage business strategy · brands & services · sales planning · buying & sourcing · sales execution · logistics · marketing & customer service — and **Management and Support Processes (8–14)** — HR · IT · finance · assets & properties · environmental health & safety · external relationships · **knowledge and change**. *(Note **change management appears as a standard enterprise process** in its own right.)*

**SCOR is based on five distinct management processes:**
$$\textbf{Plan} \cdot \textbf{Source} \cdot \textbf{Make} \cdot \textbf{Deliver} \cdot \textbf{Return}$$
**Source → Make → Deliver** is the physical flow, **Return** the reverse flow, and **Plan** sits *above* all four. The model spans **suppliers' supplier → supplier → your company → customer → customer's customer**, with the four operational processes **repeating at every link** — which is the ERP II idea of optimising the whole network.

**THE NOTATION STANDARDS:**

| Standard | Owner and detail |
|---|---|
| **EPC** — Event Driven Process Chains | Developed by **IDS Scheer** to illustrate **SAP** processes within the **ARIS** framework; now **one of the leading standards** |
| **BPMN** — Business Process Model and Notation | Developed by **BPMI**, maintained by **OMG since the 2005 merger**; **strongly IT-oriented**; provides a graphical notation for a **Business Process Diagram (BPD)** based on flowcharting; **maps to BPEL** |
| **UML** | For **object modelling in software engineering**; compiled by **three OO methodologists within Rational Software**; supported by the **Rational Unified Process** |

**BPMN's significance:** it *"supports business process management for both technical and business users… **intuitive to business users yet able to represent complex process semantics**"* and **bridges the communication gap between business process design and implementation** — because a BPMN diagram can be **mapped to an execution language (BPEL) and actually run**.

**THE FIVE DIMENSIONS of a process model (G-R-I-O-A):** **Graphical** *(pictorial representation)* · **Resource** *(define all resources so they can be associated)* · **Information** *(a view of data and how it is used)* · **Organization** *(definition and structure of organization units)* · **Analysis** *(key process metrics and attributes defined and analyzed)*

**THE MATURITY CONTINUUM** runs from **basic process flows** *(benefit: technical and business speak the same language; lowest effort)* → **add organization elements** *(organizational impacts)* → **add resources and controls** *(audit and compliance alignment)* → **add infrastructure and data** *(systems and data requirements; **data confidentiality issues**)* → **add timings and costs** *(time and cost visibility; **highest effort — time and motion studies**)*.

**The continuum is a warning as much as a roadmap: model to the depth your purpose requires, and no further.**

items.q: **What is Business Modelling? How does it differ from BPM? Describe process modelling software and its capabilities.**
items.answer:
**BUSINESS MODELLING — definition:**
> *"A **visual representation of an enterprise's business as one large system** showing different **subsystems**, what processes they support, and the **interconnection** between them, and showing **how data is flowing** between different subsystems."*

It **visually shows what will be the future application landscape** — *"ERP will take care of which processes, **where legacy applications will remain**, how data flow will happen between ERP's different modules and legacy applications."* It **can be done with any level of detailing**, and **needs to be done keeping the company's business strategy, long term goal and vision in mind**.

**BM vs BPM:**

| | **BPM** | **BM** |
|---|---|---|
| **Models** | **one process** | **the whole enterprise as one large system** |
| **Shows** | activities, steps, data flows, who does what | **subsystems and their interconnections** |
| **Answers** | *how does this process work?* | *what will the **application landscape** look like?* |

**BM's distinctive contribution is showing the boundary of the ERP** — what it absorbs and what remains legacy. That matters because *"complex interfaces"* is a named implementation challenge, and Agilent's **2,200 legacy applications** is what happens when nobody has drawn one.

**PROCESS MODELLING SOFTWARE — why it is needed:** *"the number of processes is quite large even for a medium sized company — **40 to 100**! Designing the processes is both **tedious and error prone**."*

**Capabilities:** **multi-dimension modelling** · **simulation** *(statistical, visual)* · **pre-built templates** *(industry standard frameworks — SCOR, APQC)* · **import/export**

**Vendors:** **Visio · IDS Scheer ARIS · IBM's WebSphere Business Modeler**. Many ERP products provide BPM capability themselves as **Extended ERP** — **started by Orgware of Baan ERP**. Third-party business modelling tools include **BPWIN, ER/Studio Business Architect, Oracle BPA Suite, IBM BPM**; they **link with one or more ERPs for exporting BPs**, can **input to implementation methodologies**, **allow validation of flows and alignment to business rules**, and **provide a repository of reference models**.

**On tools:** *"even the simple tool Visio can be used… **but the semantic support is very limited** — it is used only from a diagramming point. But niche products such as **ARIS have basic BP knowledge**."* Visio draws boxes; ARIS knows a box is a *process* and can therefore validate the model.

**Two further points:**

**"BPM can be helpful in selecting the ERP!"** — model your processes first, then choose the package that supports them best. This addresses the BPR risk that *"there is no guarantee those best-designed processes will be supported by the ERP solution."*

**Integrated data modelling** is *"needed **minimally**, for customization sake"* — because **"ERP is a business aware application"** and already has a data model. *"A lot of caution is required because of interdependency"*, and development must be **controlled and well managed from a maintenance and ERP upgrade point of view.**
